title: Justin's Sunday (First Apology 65–67)
hook: read his whole description of a second-century Mass
tomorrow: what do you do with a dragon lying under your ladder?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Polycarp: eighty-six years of serving Christ, and a church that wrote his story down for every church to hear. The line was the oldest story.

Rumors grow fastest around a closed door. Outsiders whispered about what Christians did when they met. So a teacher named Justin did something bold: he wrote the whole gathering out, step by step, and addressed it to the emperor. Readings, preaching, prayers, bread and wine, one loud Amen, a collection. Nothing hidden. Was that wise? Christians have answered that two ways.
screen: `RUMORS AROUND A CLOSED DOOR.` → `WRITTEN OUT FOR THE EMPEROR.` → `WAS THAT WISE?`

segments.voice: First, what Justin wrote. In the old Schaff translation: "And on the day called Sunday, all who live in cities or in the country gather together to one place, and the memoirs of the apostles or the writings of the prophets are read, as long as time permits." Then the one presiding urges everyone to imitate what they heard. All stand and pray. Bread and a cup of wine mixed with water are brought, the presider gives thanks at length, and the people answer: Amen. Justin says this food is called the Eucharist, and it isn't received as common bread. Deacons carry a share to anyone who couldn't come, and the collection goes to orphans, widows, the sick, prisoners and strangers. Second, the case for the open door. Justin wanted the rumors gone. Let outsiders see it plainly, and they'll find nothing to fear. Third, the case for the veil. Some later teachers chose differently. Cyril of Jerusalem, teaching people preparing for baptism, asked them not to repeat the mysteries to outsiders. Not to hide anything shameful, but because some holy things are better met than described. Fourth, where Catholics stand now. Both instincts live in the Mass. The doors are open, and anyone may come and watch every step. Communion itself is for Catholics prepared to receive it. And the Catechism quotes Justin's description when it explains the Mass.
screen: `CITY AND COUNTRY, ONE PLACE.` · `THE OPEN DOOR: NOTHING TO FEAR.` · `THE VEIL: BETTER MET THAN TOLD.` · `BOTH LIVE IN THE MASS.` · then, large: `THE SAME SUNDAY.`

segments.voice: On a scrap of paper, write Justin's steps down the left side: readings, preaching, prayers, bread and wine, the Amen, the gift. Down the right, write what you remember from the last Mass or gathering you went to. Draw a line wherever the two match.
Justin's Sunday. A Christian gathering written out in full, so outsiders could see there was nothing to fear.
Keep this: the same sunday, read out to an emperor, still recognizable in a parish this week. Go well.

fork.setup: your friend says the Mass should be explained to anyone, anytime, the way Justin did. you're asked to give the best case for the other side. what is it?
options: some holy things are better met than described.
outsiders can't be trusted to understand the truth.
secrecy makes people curious, so more of them join.
fork.reveal: Cyril of Jerusalem asked people preparing for baptism not to repeat the mysteries to outsiders, out of reverence, not suspicion. Catholics keep both: open doors, and Communion for those prepared.

original.note: Greek for thanksgiving: Justin says this is what the food is called among Christians.

chat.says: abuela can't get to church yet, so someone brings her communion. and mia wants to come sunday. allowed?
options: Yes. Deacons carried it to the absent back then too; Mia can watch it all, just not receive.
No. Mass is only for baptized Catholics, so Mia would have to wait outside.
Sure, and she should take Communion too, so she doesn't feel left out.
chat.meaning: Justin's deacons carried the Eucharist to those who couldn't come, and he described the whole gathering to outsiders. Doors open; Communion for Catholics prepared to receive.

Justin.meaning: an early Christian teacher who wrote to the emperor defending Christians

Eucharist.meaning: from the Greek for thanksgiving; the blessed bread and wine

Deacons.meaning: ministers who serve; here they carry the Eucharist to the absent

Cyril of Jerusalem.meaning: a bishop who taught people preparing for baptism

Catechism.meaning: the book summarizing the Catholic Church's teaching

notes: Confirm the First Apology 67 wording against the Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (Schaff edition).

Paraphrased from chs. 65–67: the ANF calls the leader 'the president'; the script says 'the one presiding' / 'the presider'. Confirm: wine mixed with water; deacons carry portions to the absent; the collection for orphans, widows, the sick, those in bonds and strangers.

The index hook says 'second-century Mass'; under the claims rule the script gives no date. 'Rumors' about Christian gatherings: the Apology answers accusations against Christians; confirm the framing is fair.

Debate: Cyril of Jerusalem, Procatechesis 12, asks catechumens not to tell the mysteries to outsiders (the 'discipline of the secret'). Paraphrased; confirm the reference and that 'better met than described' is fair as a summary of the reason (reverence).
'Communion itself is for Catholics prepared to receive it': the Church's norm, stated simply; confirm wording, and that 'anyone may come and watch' is acceptable.
CCC 1345 quotes Justin's description; confirm the paragraph number.
